doc.title: Kent Jordan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 22, 2006

title: Musicianship, craftsmanship and Yvonne Bush
summary: Realness in music and fundamentals being lost; Yvonne Bush as a band director who taught many New Orleans musicians.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: Yeah. Somehow we can get back to — I don’t know see for me music is just real. It has to have a certain, not a surrealness about it but a realness about it, that can make you feel something, really make you feel something. And I hope that we can regain that. Because truly I can tell you there was certain things that were happening even musically, as great as it is musically there were certain things that were not happening that needed to happen musically that we needed to, in a way, refocus on, you know refocus in on and try to find that verve again. Try to find that character. Because we were just sort of like floating out there, not really taking care of the kind of business that we need to take care of. Now I’m not talking about business in the sense of business sense but a sense of great musicianship. Playing in tune. Reading music. Fundamental things that my dad talks about all the time. That was being lost I’m telling you. You know you go listen to a marching band in New Orleans and it sounded like man —

Yeah where’s the craftsmanship? You know. Where is the musicianship? You know what are they learning. You see I’m telling you man a long time ago with these band directors, you have to play in tune, you have to play correctly, you have to have good posture, good musicianship. I mean man it was just like I’m sure if you haven’t, just ask any New Orleanean about Yvonne Bush. I don’t know if you’ve ever heard her but she was a preeminent band director who taught all of the musicians in New Orleans from everybody who played with Fats Domino to you know Ellis Marsalis, Harold Batiste, I mean Yvonne Bush. I’m telling you man. And so when you saw them lose that kind of direction in terms of what you’re doing and these kids are going to these schools and not really learning like what you said the craftsmanship, a lot is lost, a lot is lost. So we’re trying to find our way.
